title: VeriPlan: Integrating Formal Verification and LLMs into End-User Planning
authors: Lee, C. P.; Porfirio, D.; Wang, X. J.; Zhao, K. C.; Mutlu, B.
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
tldr: Introduces VeriPlan, a system that applies model checking to verify and refine LLM-generated plans against user-defined constraints, improving perceived output quality and user satisfaction.
problem_and_motivation: LLMs show promise for end-user planning but suffer from consistency, accuracy, and trust issues, and lack reliable self-verification. Traditional planning tools are inaccessible to everyday users due to complex formal languages. There is a need for systems that combine LLM accessibility with formal verification to ensure reliable, user-aligned planning outputs.
approach: Uses GPT-4 as the LLM planner to generate initial plans from natural language prompts.
Implements a rule translator that maps user constraints from natural language to LTL properties via a predefined temporal constraint template.
Provides flexibility sliders that allow users to adjust the strictness (hard/soft) of each constraint.
Employs the PRISM model checker to formally verify LLM-generated plans against the translated LTL constraints.
Feeds verification feedback (violated rules) back to the LLM for iterative plan regeneration.
Conducts a within-subjects ablation study (n=12) comparing the full VeriPlan system against versions lacking the rule translator or flexibility sliders.
Evaluates user experience using the USE questionnaire and the FATE performance scale.
Analyzes interview data using thematic analysis to gain qualitative insights.
findings: num: Full VeriPlan significantly outperformed the no-translator (p=.0011) and no-features (p=.0013) conditions in perceived LLM performance.
num: Full VeriPlan was significantly more useful than conditions without sliders (p=.047), without translator (p=.009), and without features (p=.0257).
num: Full VeriPlan was significantly more satisfying than the no-translator (p=.007) and no-features (p=.0101) conditions.
The rule translator improved performance, satisfaction, and usefulness by enabling user control over rigidity and aligning expectations.
Flexibility sliders showed potential to improve usefulness, especially for adaptive scenarios requiring personalization.
The model checker improved efficiency and transparency, acting as a safety net that enabled creative exploration.
Users desired actionable suggestions from the model checker, such as constraint adjustments or rephrasing guidance.
The mind map-based interface supported usability by helping users understand planning content and apply feedback.
User control over verification enforces rigidity, while control over strictness enables flexibility and creativity in planning.
Model checking provides deterministic boundaries for probabilistic LLMs, enhancing reliability and user confidence.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a novel system, VeriPlan, that integrates formal verification with large language models for end-user planning, demonstrating the viability of model checking as a guardrail for LLM outputs. It provides empirical evidence through a user study that verification and user control features significantly enhance user-perceived performance, satisfaction, and usefulness of LLMs in planning contexts. The work also offers a template-based approach for translating natural language constraints into formal logic (LTL), reducing the technical barrier for user engagement. Finally, it contributes design implications for integrating verification methods and user control features into future AI systems, emphasizing the importance of deterministic boundaries for probabilistic models.
directly_justifies: Model checking improves user experience with LLMs in planning tasks.
User control over constraint verification enforces rigidity in LLMs.
Control over strictness enables flexibility and creativity in planning.
Verification helped align expectations and refine prompts.
Model checking provides deterministic boundaries for probabilistic LLM systems.
limits: The types of temporal constraints available are a limited subset, not covering all possible user needs.
The modeling framework (PRISM/Stormpy) restricts the logical expressions that can be formulated in LTL.
The evaluation is limited to only three planning scenarios.
Sample size is limited to 12 participants.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan across all topic domains was performed. Domains related to planning constraints (7.A, 7.C, 7.D, 7.E), user trust (10.B), user engagement (11.A, 11.B), and evaluation frameworks (12.A, 12.B, 12.C) were flagged as highly relevant due to the paper's direct focus on verifying LLM-generated plans with user-defined constraints and its rigorous user study. The domains of budget-specific recommendations (7.B) and anomaly detection (8.A, 8.B, 8.C) were considered but assigned lower relevance due to the paper's general planning context, though the methodology could be applied to those areas. Behavioral profiling (5.A, 5.B, 5.C) was considered borderline; while the cold-start problem (5.B) is addressed through user-defined rules, the paper does not model financial behavior profiles or use classification, hence the low relevance scores. Mobile-first design (9.A, 9.B) and data privacy (10.A) were rejected as direct topics, as they are not core to the paper's contribution. The overall coverage is strongest in constrained optimization, evaluation methodologies, and human-AI interaction aspects.

limitations: Limited set of temporal constraints in the template.
PRISM/Stormpy restricts expressiveness of LTL logic.
